clusters.name: Father's remarriage and stepfather tension, 1987
clusters.reason: Around the time your stepfather's marriage began to separate over starting a family, you made the chess squad and felt out of your depth. Your relationship with your stepfather was distant while you leaned toward your father; anxiety rose as you struggled at the bottom of the ladder.

clusters.name: Grandfather's death and collapse of direction, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Your grandfather died in mid-1991 and your grandmother was treated for a thyroid tumour around the same time. Between your father's grandfather coming back into the family in 1989 and your own mother's wedding to Desmond in late 1992, you dropped chess and debate, started late nights, moved through the rebuilt house with Desmond's children, and leaned hard on Rafe at conservatory before a wrist injury stopped your playing. You fell into conflict with Rafe and sank into getting high and fixing radios. By early 1992 you were lost and low with no footing. Your functioning fell and anxiety rose through this stretch. A cousin was treated for melanoma around 1994. You pulled out of this when you found your drive again through the Lisbon exchange and your film work.

clusters.name: Insomnia and performance peak with Joelle, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: You bonded with Joelle around early 1998 and over the next year you played the best you ever had, winning competitions. At the same time insomnia began getting in the way before concerts though you practised hard. You separated from her in mid-1999 and started therapy with Victor Halloran after the split.

clusters.name: Burnout, grandmother's decline and depression after Marisol, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 you began running out of steam for performing and were less content by the month. Your grandmother was found to have bowel cancer, the year uncertain but running alongside your burnout. In early 2002 you had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing. You were on poor terms with family and friends and left Thornbury for Gull Harbour. You met Marisol at a winter party in early 2003, moved with her to Fenwick by mid-year, but separated within the year. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home. Once you split from Marisol that winter you sank into a deep depression; at the bottom you hardly moved from the sofa. You could not face your family; they seemed a world away. You relied on friends—Corbin, Dale, Hamish, Silas—rather than relatives. By January 2004 you began swimming laps to help you sleep and requested help from your parents with therapy costs. You returned to Victor Halloran and your functioning began to climb. Your grandmother died in February 2004. Your anxiety was high around visiting her sickroom hung over on the way to the airport; you cut it short and regret it.

clusters.name: Grandmother's death and cutoff from mother during nursing school, 2008–2010
clusters.reason: Your grandmother Lorna died in January 2008 and your grandfather Clifford died around the same time or shortly after. That July you spent four weeks building at Alder Creek with Silas before nursing school. You were too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed you to visit and you told her repeatedly the timing was wrong, but she drove out anyway. The visit went wrong and you kept the door shut on her. When you left for nursing school in Marlow Sound in August you stopped speaking to your mother; the silence held roughly a year. Your aunt had a stroke in early 2009 with months of rehabilitation. Your partner's brother's first child was born in 2010.

clusters.name: Marriage to Wren and tension in her family, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: You married Wren in March 2017 and saw your mother a bit less once she came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in October 2017. Your sister Tara married James and flies for a regional airline; your aunt's memory slipping grew worse and she began lashing out when muddled. In late 2019 Wren was swamped—one thing after another—and your anxiety rose as you moved into overfunctioning to settle her. Her family talks all day and nothing happens to one that the others don't hear. At her mother's retirement party at the lake house in late October 2019 you awoke from the small hours with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose. Your sleep is worst around her family; you feel you don't belong. At the same time your own job steadied and paid well, your anxiety had dropped, but by October you felt constantly you ought to be driving your projects forward. You started a sleeping pill. You aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother to soften the distance. A baby was on the way for your sister.
